questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
options: They are the same thing
An image is an immutable, layered template; a container is a running (or stopped) instance of it
A container is a compressed image
An image runs on Linux only; a container runs anywhere
questions.explanation: You can start many containers from one image. Each container adds a thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers, and that layer disappears when the container is removed.

questions.question: Why do Dockerfiles copy the dependency file (`requirements.txt`, `uv.lock`) and install dependencies before copying the source code?
options: Docker requires this order
So the dependency layer stays cached when only the code changes, which makes rebuilds fast
To make the image smaller
To run the tests first
questions.explanation: Each instruction creates a layer, and a layer is rebuilt when its inputs change, along with every layer after it. Code changes often and dependencies rarely, so installing dependencies first avoids reinstalling them on every build.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a multi-stage Docker build?
options: It runs several containers at once
Build tools stay in the builder stage; only the runtime artifacts are copied into a smaller, safer final image
It builds for several CPU architectures
It avoids writing a Dockerfile
questions.explanation: Compilers, headers and caches are not needed at runtime. Leaving them out reduces image size and attack surface, which is also why you should run as a non-root user.

questions.question: An image has `ENTRYPOINT ["pipeline"]` and `CMD ["ingest"]`. What does `docker run image migrate` execute?
options: `ingest`
`pipeline ingest`
`pipeline migrate`
`migrate`
questions.explanation: The ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable; CMD provides default arguments, which are replaced by the arguments you pass to `docker run`.

questions.question: A PostgreSQL container is removed and recreated. How do you keep the data?
options: Data is always kept inside the image
Mount a volume on the data directory
Use a bigger container
Commit the container to a new image after each write
questions.explanation: The container's writable layer is ephemeral. Volumes live outside the container lifecycle. Note that `docker compose down -v` deletes volumes too.

questions.question: What is a Pod in Kubernetes?
options: A physical server of the cluster
The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage
A Docker image stored in the cluster
A group of nodes
questions.explanation: Containers in a pod share an IP and can share volumes; usually a pod runs one main container, sometimes with sidecars. Pods are disposable: controllers such as Deployments recreate them.

questions.question: Pods get a new IP address each time they are recreated. What gives clients a stable address that load-balances across them?
options: A Deployment
A Service
A ConfigMap
A PersistentVolume
questions.explanation: A Service selects pods by label and exposes a stable virtual IP and DNS name. The Deployment manages the pods' replicas and rollouts, not how they are reached.

questions.question: What happens when a pod's readiness probe fails, compared with its liveness probe?
options: Both restart the container
Readiness failing stops traffic to the pod; liveness failing restarts the container
Readiness failing deletes the pod; liveness failing only logs a warning
They do the same thing on different ports
questions.explanation: Readiness answers "can I receive traffic now?" (e.g. while a model is loading). Liveness answers "am I stuck?" and triggers a restart. A too-strict liveness probe causes restart loops.

questions.question: Order the steps of releasing a new version with a Kubernetes Deployment.
steps: Build the image with a new, unique tag
Push it to a container registry
Update the image tag in the Deployment and apply it
Kubernetes starts new pods and waits for them to be ready
Old pods are terminated progressively (rolling update)
questions.explanation: Unique tags (not `latest`) make rollouts and rollbacks explicit. Readiness probes are what keep traffic away from new pods until they are ready.

questions.question: Order the instructions of a well-structured Dockerfile for a Python app.
steps: Start from a slim base image
questions.explanation: Order instructions from least to most frequently changed so the cache is reused. Running as non-root limits the damage if the app is compromised.
